text: Limpho Hani (née Sekamane; born 31 January 1948) is a Mosotho–South African activist and the widow of anti-apartheid activist Chris Hani. Born in Sea Point, Maseru, the capital of Lesotho, she married Chris Hani in 1974 at a magistrate's court in Lusaka, Zambia, with a celebratory wedding lunch at Wimpy. After returning to Southern Africa in late 1975, the couple moved into a house in Lithabaneng, Maseru, known as "Moscow House" by ANC members. They had three daughters: Neo (born 1973), Nomakhwezi (born 1978, died 2001), and Lindiwe (born 1981). Hani worked for the Lesotho Tourism Board but became increasingly involved in Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK) operations, including smuggling new MK recruits across the South African border through Swaziland after the 1976 Soweto Uprising. She was detained by South African authorities from 1977 to 1978 and, according to her husband's biographer Hugh Macmillan, gave evidence against Mountain Qumbela, a former ANC leader in the Cape. In 1982, after her husband faced an assassination attempt, she left her job to move with him to Lusaka. She returned to Maseru in 1984, working first with the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency and then at the Swedish Embassy from 1985. The couple moved to South Africa in 1990 after the ANC was unbanned. On 10 April 1993, Chris Hani was assassinated outside their home in Dawn Park, Boksburg, with his teenage daughter Nomakhwezi present. In the April 1994 post-apartheid elections, Hani was elected as an ANC Member of the National Assembly and re-elected in June 1999, resigning from her seat on 17 August 1999, when it was filled by Kay Moonsamy. She also served on the ANC's National Executive Committee, first elected at the 49th National Conference in Bloemfontein in December 1994 and re-elected in December 1997, before resigning during her second term due to other commitments. Following her husband's murder, Hani refused to forgive the killers, a stance described by Sisonke Msimang as "almost heretical" in contrast to Nelson Mandela's conciliatory approach. During the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Janusz Waluś and Clive Derby-Lewis expressed regret and applied for amnesty, but Hani and her family, represented by George Bizos, opposed amnesty. In 2014, when a court approved medical parole for Derby-Lewis, Hani expressed outrage, calling it "a very sad day in South Africa." In 2022, Waluś was granted parole after a sustained campaign by Hani and the SACP to block it. In a media statement, Hani said that Waluś murdered her husband and daughter, and that he had not apologized to her, stating she would never forgive him and only sought justice. The Constitutional Court ruled in November 2022 that the Minister of Justice and Correctional Services had been irrational in denying parole to Waluś, who had been eligible for release for over 15 years. Hani stormed out of the court, calling the verdict "diabolical" and accusing the court and Chief Justice Raymond Zondo of failing South Africa, saying, "This country is finished. In this country, a foreign white [Polish Waluś] can come into South Africa and kill my husband." She expressed sympathy with Minister Lindiwe Sisulu, whom she said was "the only one in this country who saw through these guys." A subsequent application by Hani and the SACP to rescind the court's order was unanimously dismissed.
